text:
I want to explore an AI tool that helps government agencies understand what needs to change when legislation, regulations or whole-of-government policies are updated. At the moment, staff often rely on emails, spreadsheets and individual knowledge to work out which internal policies, guidance, forms, systems and operational processes may be affected. This can take weeks and creates a risk that important dependencies are missed.

The tool would compare a new or amended requirement against an agency’s existing documents and produce a draft impact map. It would identify potentially affected obligations, documents, processes and business owners, explain why each item may be relevant and link its suggestions back to the source text. Policy, legal, compliance and operational staff could then review the map, reject false matches and assign confirmed actions.

It would use public legislation and policy material together with approved, unclassified internal documents. It would not provide authoritative legal advice, decide whether the agency is compliant or automatically change policies or systems. Human experts would remain responsible for interpreting requirements and approving any action. I imagine starting with one narrow policy area in a single agency to test whether the tool finds meaningful dependencies that staff would otherwise miss.

This sounds like a powerful way to reduce the 'institutional memory' bottleneck in policy implementation. I've drafted the core sections based on your description; to help us refine the scope, how do you envision the tool handling the 'versioning' of internal documents to ensure it's always comparing against the current state of the agency?

The tool should compare new requirements against a dated snapshot of the agency’s current, approved document set. Wherever possible, documents would come from an authoritative repository and retain metadata such as owner, approval status, version number, effective date and review date.

The AI should not silently decide which of several conflicting copies is current. If it finds duplicates, drafts or unclear version histories, it should flag them and ask an authorised user to confirm the version to include. Each impact map should record exactly which document versions were analysed so the result can be reproduced later.

When an internal document is updated, the tool would preserve the previous analysis and show what changed in the impact map rather than overwriting it. For an initial proof of concept, we could avoid live integration and use a manually curated, approved document set frozen at a nominated date.

That approach to versioning—treating the repository as a 'frozen' snapshot—is a smart way to manage risk and ensure auditability. Since we're prioritizing accuracy over live integration for the POC, how do you plan to handle the 'feedback loop' where the AI learns from the user's corrections to reduce false positives in future runs?

For the proof of concept, reviewers would mark each suggested dependency as confirmed, incorrect or uncertain, and could edit the explanation or identify a missed dependency. They would also select a reason for corrections—for example, similar terminology but different purpose, superseded material, incorrect business owner or an overly broad interpretation.

Individual feedback would not automatically retrain or alter the tool. Corrections would be recorded in an auditable feedback set and reviewed periodically by the project team and relevant subject-matter experts. Agreed patterns could then be used to refine the retrieval rules, prompts or matching thresholds before the next controlled run.

We would maintain a fixed set of test examples and rerun them after each change to check whether false positives fall without increasing missed dependencies. Results would be tracked using measures such as the proportion of suggestions confirmed by reviewers, false positives by category and important dependencies found only by humans. Agency-specific corrections would remain separate from any more general improvements.

Your 'human-in-the-loop' feedback strategy is excellent for maintaining auditability and preventing model drift. Given this rigorous approach to validation, how do you plan to handle the 'cold start' problem—how will you seed the initial retrieval rules or prompts to ensure the first set of results is useful enough for staff to bother reviewing?

We would seed the proof of concept using a small set of historical policy or legislative changes whose impacts are already understood. Subject-matter experts would select around 10–15 examples and document the internal policies, processes and owners that were genuinely affected. This would create a “gold standard” against which the tool’s first results could be tested.

The initial retrieval approach would also use an agency-specific glossary, document metadata and a simple map of business functions and owners. Results would be ranked by confidence and supported by direct quotations from both the new requirement and the potentially affected document. Staff would initially see only a manageable number of the strongest matches rather than a long, unfiltered list.

Before live testing, the team would compare the tool’s results with the expert mappings and adjust its instructions, search approach and thresholds. We would proceed only if the first output finds a useful proportion of known dependencies and reviewers judge that checking the suggestions takes less effort than starting from scratch. Early use would remain a supervised calibration exercise rather than operational reliance.

Using a 'gold standard' set of historical changes is a perfect way to calibrate the system before it touches live policy. Since you're focusing on a manageable number of high-confidence matches, how do you plan to handle the 'long tail' of dependencies—the subtle, low-confidence links that might be critical but are easily missed by a threshold-based system?
